content: Tuberculosis (TB) is a disease caused by a bacterium known as Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Individuals with TB can transmit the bacteria to others through the air when they cough, speak, or sing. Infection occurs when a person inhales TB bacteria into their lungs. Once in the lungs, the bacteria can disseminate through the bloodstream to infect other parts of the body, such as the kidneys, spine, or brain. Symptoms of TB disease in the lungs include a persistent cough lasting three weeks or longer, chest pain, coughing up blood or mucus, fatigue or weakness, weight loss, loss of appetite, and night sweats. If TB infects other parts of the body, symptoms will vary depending on the affected area. Not everyone infected with TB bacteria becomes ill or exhibits symptoms. Individuals with latent TB infection harbor the bacteria in their bodies but do not show symptoms and cannot spread the disease to others. However, latent TB can progress to active TB disease if the immune system becomes weakened. People with latent TB infection can take medication to prevent the development of active TB disease. TB occurs worldwide but is more prevalent in certain regions, including sub-Saharan Africa, Eastern Europe, and Asia. Drug-resistant TB is relatively rare. Travelers planning to work in healthcare settings should consult infection control or occupational health experts in the destination country before engaging in patient care. Individuals with weakened immune systems, particularly those with HIV infection, are at significantly higher risk of developing TB disease compared to those with healthy immune systems. Travelers can take specific measures to protect themselves from TB. These include avoiding prolonged close contact with individuals who may have TB, especially in crowded environments such as clinics, hospitals, prisons, or homeless shelters. Travelers should also avoid close contact with people who are coughing or appear unwell and take extra precautions around individuals known to have TB. Those working in healthcare settings should consult infection control or occupational health experts about preventive measures, such as wearing an N95 respirator. They should also consider being tested for TB infection before leaving the United States. While a TB vaccine exists, the CDC does not recommend it for travelers.
